Hinged Tessellation 2

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Squares and triangles are joined like hinges to make a repeating pattern.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B and C, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Try the two preset buttons and the Layers and Colour choices to see how the pattern changes.
Colour
Look for the math

The page shows a tessellation that can bend without breaking: the pieces stay whole, but their arrangement changes. Two sibling applets make different choices about which pieces stay rigid.

Five pieces at one corner

The page calls the starting pattern (4, 3, 3, 4, 3) because five regular polygons meet at every corner: a square, then two triangles, then a square and one more triangle. A square corner contributes 90° and an equilateral triangle corner 60°, so

90° + 60° + 60° + 90° + 60° = 360°.

That is exactly a full turn, which is why the pieces fit with no gap around the point A. The logic test checks these five angles at the starting hinge.

What the hinges keep fixed

Drag A, B or C. The fourth corner D is placed so that ABCD is a parallelogram: D = A + C − B. Every side is then turned through a quarter turn to build the squares around it; a quarter turn keeps equal sides and right angles, so the squares really are squares at every position. This is applet B: it frees the triangles and keeps the squares. Applet A makes the opposite choice, freeing the squares into rhombi while keeping the triangles equilateral.

Why the pieces always still fit

With Lock hinges on, A and C stay on circles centred at B, so BA = BC. Write β for the angle at A of the triangle ABC. The matching triangle ACD also has angle β at A, and the third triangle at A has angle 180° − 2β. The two square corners add another 180°, so the five angles at A are always

90° + β + β + 90° + (180° − 2β) = 360°.

The logic test checks all 175 whole-degree hinges from 3° to 177°: the five angles fill a turn every time, and the triangles are equilateral only at β = 60°. With Lock hinges off, BA and BC may differ and the triangles become scalene — the page's further relaxation to parallelograms — yet the five angles still add to 360°.

The square derivative

Press Squares 90°. Now the apex at B is a right angle, so β = 45°: ABC and ACD are right isosceles and together make a square, while the third triangle is right isosceles too and pairs with its neighbour. Four squares meet at each corner: the page's derivative of the (4, 4, 4, 4) tessellation. The logic test confirms this and also checks that choosing 60° restores the semi-regular start. Two harmless quirks of the original are kept in the core but never drawn: an unused signed angle computed by the motif routine, and a second layer-growing routine that the applet never calls.

Lock the hinges, press Squares 90°, then drag B a little: the pattern stays gap-free even though no triangle is equilateral any more.
